questions.question: How do you manage configuration with ConfigMaps and Secrets for a Spring Boot application in Kubernetes?
questions.title: ConfigMaps and Secrets: Spring Boot Config Management in Kubernetes
questions.direct_answer: ConfigMaps hold non-sensitive config injected as env (`envFrom`) or mounted as files; Secrets hold credentials, base64-encoded at rest and gated by RBAC + etcd encryption. Spring Boot picks them up automatically via relaxed binding (`SPRING_DATASOURCE_URL` → `spring.datasource.url`) — same image runs in dev/stage/prod. Updating a ConfigMap does **not** restart pods; use Reloader, checksum annotations, or Spring Cloud Kubernetes for reloads. For production credentials prefer External Secrets Operator syncing from Vault or cloud secret managers.

interviewer_intent.testing: Practical config management for production Spring Boot deployments
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Putting credentials in ConfigMaps, expecting env-var reload on ConfigMap change, or treating base64 as encryption
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain relaxed binding, property source precedence, immutable ConfigMaps, Spring Cloud Kubernetes with `@RefreshScope`, Reloader, External Secrets Operator, and etcd encryption-at-rest

sections.title: The Gap Between 'Works Locally' and 'Works in Kubernetes': Configuration Injection
sections.content:
Every Spring Boot application carries configuration — database URLs, log levels, API keys, feature flags. Locally these live in `application.properties` or `application.yml` inside the JAR. In Kubernetes, the same application must run in dev, staging, and production from the same Docker image. **The image never changes; only the configuration changes.**

Kubernetes provides two primitives: **ConfigMaps** for non-sensitive data and **Secrets** for credentials. Spring Boot's externalized configuration makes the integration seamless — environment variables injected from ConfigMaps and Secrets override values baked into `application.properties` via property source precedence. No code changes, no conditional logic, no environment-specific builds.

**Two traps catch every team:**

- Treating ConfigMaps and Secrets interchangeably — ConfigMaps are plain text in etcd, readable by anyone with namespace access. Putting a DB password in a ConfigMap means every dev with `kubectl get configmap` can see it.
- Assuming a ConfigMap update auto-reloads running pods — it does not. Env vars are frozen at container start.

sections.title: How Config Flows From Kubernetes Into the JVM Process
sections.content:
The same Spring Boot JAR reads config from multiple sources in a defined precedence order. Kubernetes injects at the environment level, overriding packaged defaults.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    CM[ConfigMap\nspring-app-config] -->|envFrom| Pod[Pod: spring-app container]
    SEC[Secret\nspring-app-secrets] -->|envFrom| Pod
    VAULT[Vault / AWS Secrets Manager] --> ESO[External Secrets Operator] --> SEC
    Pod --> ENV[OS env vars\nSPRING_DATASOURCE_URL]
    ENV -->|overrides| JAR[application.properties\npackaged defaults]
    JAR --> CTX[Spring Environment\n@Value / @ConfigurationProperties]
    CM -.volume mount.-> FILE[/config/application.yml]
    FILE -->|spring.config.import| CTX
    RL[Reloader controller] -. watches .-> CM
    RL -. watches .-> SEC
    RL -->|triggers rollout| Deploy[Deployment]
```

Spring reads env vars first (highest priority), then mounted files via `spring.config.import=configtree:/config/`, then packaged `application.properties` as the fallback. **Same JAR, different env produces different runtime behavior.**

sections.title: Spring Boot Relaxed Binding: Zero Code for Env-to-Property Translation
sections.content:
Spring Boot's **relaxed binding** translates env var names to property paths automatically. The convention is mechanical: dots become underscores, everything uppercase. `SPRING_DATASOURCE_URL` maps to `spring.datasource.url`. `MY_APP_MAX_CONNECTIONS` maps to `my.app.max-connections`. ConfigMap keys follow standard Kubernetes `SCREAMING_CASE` without adapter code.

```yaml
containers:
  - name: app
    envFrom:
      - configMapRef: {name: spring-app-config}
      - secretRef:    {name: spring-app-secrets}
```

Every key in the ConfigMap becomes an env var; Spring's property resolver picks them up at startup. Precedence: env vars override packaged `application.properties`. The JAR carries sensible dev defaults (`spring.datasource.url=jdbc:postgresql://localhost:5432/myapp`) while the ConfigMap overrides in Kubernetes (`SPRING_DATASOURCE_URL=jdbc:postgresql://postgres-svc:5432/myapp`). **Same image, different behavior, no rebuild.**

For complex nested config that does not fit flat key-value pairs, mount the ConfigMap as a file at `/config/application.yml`:

```yaml
volumes:
  - name: config
    configMap: {name: spring-app-yaml}
volumeMounts:
  - name: config
    mountPath: /config
```

Set `spring.config.import=optional:configtree:/config/` so Spring Boot loads the full YAML structure.

sections.title: The ConfigMap-Update-Doesn't-Restart-Pod Problem
sections.content:
This catches every team at least once. You update a ConfigMap with `kubectl apply`, verify the new value with `kubectl get configmap`, and running pods still use old values. **Env vars are set at container start and never re-read.** The ConfigMap source changed, but env was already injected into the running process.

Three solutions:

**1. Rolling restart via checksum annotation.** The standard Helm pattern. Embed the ConfigMap checksum in the Deployment's pod template:

```yaml
template:
  metadata:
    annotations:
      checksum/config: {{ include (print $.Template.BasePath "/configmap.yaml") . | sha256sum }}
```

Changing the ConfigMap changes the checksum, changes the pod template hash, triggers a rolling restart. **Guaranteed consistency, no special tooling inside the app.**

**2. Reloader operator (stakater/Reloader).** Annotate the Deployment `reloader.stakater.com/auto: "true"`. Reloader watches ConfigMaps and Secrets and triggers rollouts automatically on change. Language-agnostic — works for any stack.

**3. Spring Cloud Kubernetes Config.** Watches ConfigMap changes through the Kubernetes API and triggers `@RefreshScope` reload on affected beans — no restart required. Works for beans annotated `@ConfigurationProperties` or `@RefreshScope`. Does **not** work for values consumed during startup (DB pool size, Tomcat connector settings). Pair with checksum annotation for the startup-time properties.

sections.title: Why Secrets Need More Than Base64 and What To Do
sections.content:
Kubernetes Secrets are **base64-encoded, not encrypted**. Run `kubectl get secret db-secret -o jsonpath='{.data.password}' | base64 -d` and the password prints in plain text. Base64 is encoding, not security. Real security layers:

- **RBAC** — controls who can `get`/`list` Secrets in a namespace. Most developers should be denied `get` on Secrets they do not need.
- **etcd encryption at rest** — API server `EncryptionConfiguration` encrypts Secret data before writing to etcd. Without this, anyone with etcd backup access reads every Secret.
- **External secret manager** — the gold standard. Never store real secrets in Kubernetes at all.

**External Secrets Operator (ESO)** syncs Secrets from AWS Secrets Manager, HashiCorp Vault, or GCP Secret Manager into Kubernetes Secrets automatically. Rotation happens in the external manager; ESO propagates new values:

```yaml
apiVersion: external-secrets.io/v1beta1
kind: ExternalSecret
metadata: {name: db-credentials}
spec:
  refreshInterval: 1h
  secretStoreRef: {name: aws-secretsmanager, kind: SecretStore}
  target: {name: db-secret}
  data:
    - secretKey: password
      remoteRef: {key: prod/db, property: password}
```

Centralized audit, automatic rotation, access policies outside the Kubernetes RBAC boundary.

For teams not yet using an external manager, **minimum baseline**: enable etcd encryption-at-rest, restrict Secret `get` via namespace Roles, use `stringData` for plain text input (auto base64-encoded), and never commit manifests with real `stringData` to Git.

sections.title: Trade-offs: envFrom vs File Mount, Immutable ConfigMaps, GitOps Patterns
sections.content:
**envFrom vs individual env:** `envFrom` is cleaner (one ref, all keys) but loses fine-grained control — every key becomes an env var including accidentally added ones. For strict contracts, list each `env.valueFrom.configMapKeyRef` explicitly so the Deployment spec documents the exact keys required.

**Env vars vs mounted files for Secrets.** Env vars appear in `kubectl describe pod` output and in process listings (`/proc/<pid>/environ`). **Mounted files are safer** — restricted by file permissions, not visible to other processes. For production Secrets, prefer volume mounts at `/secrets/` with `spring.config.import=optional:configtree:/secrets/`.

**Immutable ConfigMaps** (`immutable: true`) improve kubelet performance for large ConfigMaps (reduces watch cache load) and prevent accidental edits. Downside: you cannot update — you must delete and recreate with a new name, updating the Deployment to reference the new name. Standard pattern with GitOps: `app-config-v17` instead of `app-config`, bumped on each change.

**GitOps pattern.** Commit ConfigMap and Deployment manifests to Git. For Secrets, use **Sealed Secrets** (Bitnami) or ESO — never commit plain Secrets. Sealed Secrets encrypts locally with the cluster's public key; only the cluster's controller can decrypt. Safe to commit to a public repo.

**ConfigMap size limits.** Each ConfigMap is limited to 1MB (etcd value size). Very large configs (e.g., bundled ML model metadata, large i18n files) should go in a volume from a PV or S3, not a ConfigMap.

**Drift detection.** In non-GitOps environments, config drift between environments is real — dev and prod ConfigMaps diverge silently. Tools like Kubernetes Configuration Drift Detection, or just `kubectl diff -f configmap.yaml` in CI, catch drift before incidents.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Spring Boot relaxed binding maps `SPRING_DATASOURCE_URL` to `spring.datasource.url`** — no code changes; ConfigMap keys in `SCREAMING_CASE` automatically override packaged defaults at startup.
- **`envFrom` injects all ConfigMap keys at once** — cleaner than per-key `env` but values are frozen at container creation and never re-read.
- **ConfigMap updates do not restart pods** — use Helm checksum annotations, Reloader operator, or Spring Cloud Kubernetes with `@RefreshScope` for live reload.
- **Secrets are base64-encoded, not encrypted** — enable etcd encryption-at-rest, restrict RBAC `get` on Secrets, and prefer External Secrets Operator syncing from Vault or cloud secret managers.
- **Mount Secrets as files, not env vars, when possible** — file mounts restricted by file permissions; env vars appear in `kubectl describe pod` and process listings.
- **Immutable ConfigMaps + versioned names for GitOps** — `app-config-v17` pattern guarantees deploy-time consistency and prevents silent in-place edits.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
ConfigMaps and Secrets both inject configuration into Pods, but they exist for different reasons: ConfigMaps for non-sensitive config, Secrets for credentials. Kubernetes handles their access control and audit differently.

**ConfigMap — non-sensitive configuration**
- Stores key-value pairs or entire files; Spring Boot reads them as env vars (`envFrom.configMapRef`) or as mounted property files via `spring.config.import=optional:configtree:/config/`.
- The configtree import mounts the ConfigMap as a directory where each key becomes a file; Spring reads nested properties from file paths — `database.url` in the ConfigMap becomes `database.url` in the Spring environment.
- Critical behavior: updating a ConfigMap does not restart running pods — env vars are frozen at container start; mounted files update eventually (within ~60s kubelet sync) but the app must watch for changes; the safest approach is a rolling restart triggered by a Helm checksum annotation or Reloader.

**Secrets — credential injection**
- Kubernetes Secrets are base64-encoded by default, not encrypted — any user with `get secret` permission can read them; base64 is encoding, not security; enable etcd encryption-at-rest and RBAC restriction to make Secrets meaningful.
- Spring Boot reads Secrets like ConfigMaps — as env vars or mounted files; prefer mounted files because env vars appear in `kubectl describe pod` and process listings.
- In production, Kubernetes-native Secrets are often insufficient — use External Secrets Operator to sync from AWS Secrets Manager, HashiCorp Vault, or GCP Secret Manager; ESO fetches and rotates without relying solely on Kubernetes RBAC.

**The environment variable reload problem**
- Neither ConfigMap nor Secret updates propagate to running containers as env vars — the container must restart to see new values.
- Reloader (stakater/Reloader) watches ConfigMap and Secret changes and triggers rolling restarts automatically — annotate the Deployment with `reloader.stakater.com/auto: "true"` and Reloader handles the rest.
- For config that can be hot-reloaded at the Spring level, use Spring Cloud Kubernetes Config with `@RefreshScope` beans — but note startup-time config (DB pool size, Tomcat connector) cannot hot-reload and still needs a pod restart.

questions.question: How do Kubernetes namespaces and RBAC support multi-team environments?
questions.title: Kubernetes Namespaces and RBAC for Multi-Team Environments
questions.direct_answer: Namespaces provide logical (not security) isolation within a cluster. RBAC controls which users and ServiceAccounts can perform which verbs on which resources in which namespaces — `Role` is namespace-scoped, `ClusterRole` is cluster-wide. Combine namespaces + RBAC + `ResourceQuota` + `LimitRange` + `NetworkPolicy` for secure, cost-bounded multi-tenancy. Enforce least privilege on ServiceAccounts so compromised pods have minimal blast radius.

interviewer_intent.testing: Understanding of multi-tenancy patterns in enterprise Kubernetes
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Giving developers cluster-admin, granting default ServiceAccount unrestricted access, or forgetting ResourceQuota so one team exhausts cluster
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Differentiate Role vs ClusterRole, show a practical developer Role, ServiceAccount hardening (`automountServiceAccountToken: false`), NetworkPolicy isolation, and `kubectl auth can-i` for effective-permission testing

sections.title: The Blast Radius Problem: What Happens When kubectl Delete Hits the Wrong Namespace
sections.content:
A developer runs `kubectl delete deployment spring-app` intending to clean up their dev environment. But their kubeconfig context was still pointed at the production namespace. The production deployment — with all its running pods — is gone. Every user gets connection errors. Recovery depends on how fast someone recreates the deployment.

This disaster is entirely preventable with **namespaces and RBAC**. Namespaces create logical boundaries: `team-payments-dev` is completely separate from `team-payments-prod`. RBAC restricts what each user or ServiceAccount can do in each namespace: developers get read-write in dev, read-only in prod.

The combination of namespaces + RBAC is what makes **multi-tenant clusters** viable. Without them, every team shares the same resource pool with unrestricted access — one team's misconfiguration takes down another. Without **ResourceQuota** (the third piece), one team can deploy 50 replicas each requesting 4GB memory and starve the scheduler, making every other team's pods unschedulable. Enterprise Kubernetes platforms enforce all three: namespace isolation, RBAC, quotas — plus a fourth: **NetworkPolicy** to prevent pod-to-pod lateral movement after compromise.

sections.title: The Multi-Tenancy Stack: Namespace + RBAC + Quota + NetworkPolicy
sections.content:
Each layer solves a different problem. Missing any one is a real vulnerability.

```mermaid
flowchart TB
    User[User: alice@company\nSSO group: team-payments-devs] --> RB[RoleBinding\nteam-payments-dev]
    RB --> Role[Role: developer\nget/list/create/delete Deployments]
    Role --> NS1[Namespace: team-payments-dev]
    User -.cannot access.-x NS2[Namespace: team-payments-prod]
    SA[ServiceAccount\npayment-api] --> RB2[RoleBinding]
    RB2 --> Role2[Role: payment-api-role\nget Secrets for DB creds only]
    Role2 --> NS1
    NS1 --> RQ[ResourceQuota\ncpu: 10, mem: 20Gi, pods: 50]
    NS1 --> LR[LimitRange\nDefault request/limit per pod]
    NS1 --> NP[NetworkPolicy\ningress: only from team-payments namespace]
    NS1 --> Pods[Pods in namespace]
    NS2 --> RQ2[Separate ResourceQuota]
    NS2 --> NP2[NetworkPolicy: deny cross-namespace]
```

Namespace isolates resources. RBAC controls who can do what. ResourceQuota controls how much. NetworkPolicy controls who talks to whom.

sections.title: Role vs ClusterRole: Namespace Boundaries as the First Line of Defense
sections.content:
Kubernetes RBAC has two scopes:

- **Role** applies within a single namespace. A Role in `team-payments-dev` that grants `create` and `delete` on Deployments only works there — the same user gets `Forbidden` in any other namespace unless granted access.
- **ClusterRole** applies cluster-wide. Used for platform admins managing nodes, namespaces, CRDs, and cluster-scoped resources (PV, StorageClass).

Least privilege means starting with namespace-scoped Roles and only creating ClusterRoles for genuine cross-namespace needs. Platform administrators need ClusterRoles. Application developers rarely do.

**Practical developer Role** — deploy and debug, but not manage Secrets or RBAC:

```yaml
apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
kind: Role
metadata: {namespace: team-payments-dev, name: developer}
rules:
  - apiGroups: ["", "apps"]
    resources: ["pods", "deployments", "services", "configmaps"]
    verbs: ["get", "list", "watch", "create", "update", "patch", "delete"]
  - apiGroups: [""]
    resources: ["pods/log", "pods/exec"]
    verbs: ["get", "create"]
```

Notice what is **missing**: no access to `secrets`, no access to `roles` or `rolebindings`. A **RoleBinding** then assigns this Role to an SSO group:

```yaml
kind: RoleBinding
metadata: {namespace: team-payments-dev, name: developers}
subjects:
  - kind: Group
    name: team-payments-devs@company.com
roleRef: {kind: Role, name: developer, apiGroup: rbac.authorization.k8s.io}
```

New team members get the right permissions automatically when added to the identity-provider group.

**Verify effective permissions before an incident:**

```bash
kubectl auth can-i create deployments -n team-payments-dev --as alice@company.com
kubectl auth can-i delete deployments -n team-payments-prod --as alice@company.com  # should say no
```

sections.title: ServiceAccount RBAC: Securing What Pods Themselves Can Do
sections.content:
**Every pod runs as a ServiceAccount.** Without explicit configuration, pods use the namespace's `default` ServiceAccount, which historically had excessive implicit permissions. The ServiceAccount's token is mounted at `/var/run/secrets/kubernetes.io/serviceaccount/token` — any library inside the container can call the Kubernetes API with that token.

**A compromised pod inherits its ServiceAccount's permissions.** If that SA can list Secrets cluster-wide, an attacker who executes code in the pod exfiltrates every Secret.

**Minimum hardening:**

- Create a dedicated ServiceAccount per workload, not shared.
- Grant only the specific permissions needed via a namespace-scoped Role.
- Set `automountServiceAccountToken: false` on pods that do NOT need Kubernetes API access (most application pods).

```yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: ServiceAccount
metadata: {namespace: team-payments-prod, name: payment-api}
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
spec:
  serviceAccountName: payment-api
  automountServiceAccountToken: false   # pod does not call K8s API
```

If the pod DOES need API access (operator, controller, Spring Cloud Kubernetes), create a Role with exactly what it needs:

```yaml
kind: Role
rules:
  - apiGroups: [""]
    resources: ["configmaps"]
    resourceNames: ["app-config"]   # only THIS configmap
    verbs: ["get", "watch"]
```

The `resourceNames` filter is critical — without it the pod can read every ConfigMap in the namespace.

sections.title: ResourceQuota and LimitRange: Preventing Cluster-Wide Starvation
sections.content:
RBAC controls what you can do. **ResourceQuota controls how much.** Without quotas, one team deploying a memory-intensive workload can exhaust the cluster, making every other team's pods `Pending` indefinitely.

```yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: ResourceQuota
metadata: {namespace: team-payments}
spec:
  hard:
    requests.cpu: "10"
    requests.memory: 20Gi
    limits.cpu: "20"
    limits.memory: 40Gi
    count/pods: "50"
    persistentvolumeclaims: "10"
```

This caps the team at 10 CPU cores of requests, 20Gi memory requests, 50 pods, 10 PVCs. Exceeding the cap rejects the creating API call with a clear error citing which quota was violated.

**`LimitRange` complements Quota** by setting per-pod defaults and maximums. Without LimitRange, a pod without resource specs gets unlimited access — a single misconfigured Deployment bypasses the entire quota system. LimitRange injects defaults into pods that do not specify them, ensuring every workload has boundaries:

```yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: LimitRange
metadata: {namespace: team-payments}
spec:
  limits:
    - type: Container
      default:        {cpu: 500m, memory: 512Mi}
      defaultRequest: {cpu: 100m, memory: 128Mi}
      max:            {cpu: 2,    memory: 4Gi}
```

Pair quotas with Prometheus alerts when a namespace reaches 80% of allocation so teams plan capacity before hitting rejections during a critical deployment.

sections.title: Hardening: NetworkPolicy, Pod Security, and Common Pitfalls
sections.content:
**NetworkPolicy — the missing isolation layer.** By default every pod in every namespace can reach every Service cluster-wide. A compromised pod in `team-marketing` can query the payment database in `team-payments`. A NetworkPolicy restricts ingress/egress:

```yaml
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata: {namespace: team-payments-prod}
spec:
  podSelector: {}    # applies to all pods
  policyTypes: [Ingress]
  ingress:
    - from:
      - namespaceSelector:
          matchLabels: {team: payments}   # only payments namespaces
```

Requires a CNI that supports NetworkPolicy (Calico, Cilium) — not all clusters have it enabled.

**Pod Security Standards (PSS).** The successor to PodSecurityPolicy. Enforced per-namespace via labels: `pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce: restricted`. Prevents privileged pods, host-path mounts, running as root — essential for untrusted workloads.

**Common pitfalls:**

- **ClusterRoleBinding for things that should be namespaced.** A ClusterRoleBinding granting `view` to all developers gives them read access to every Secret in every namespace including `kube-system`.
- **Wildcard verbs in production Roles.** `verbs: ["*"]` is often mistakenly shipped; audit with `kubectl describe role` and `rbac-lookup`.
- **Missing NetworkPolicy.** Easy to overlook until a security audit. A default-deny NetworkPolicy plus explicit allow rules is the safer posture.
- **`system:masters` kubeconfig.** The bootstrap admin kubeconfig bypasses RBAC entirely — never distribute to developers; use SSO-backed tokens instead.
- **Default ServiceAccount with mounted token.** Legacy from Kubernetes <1.24; modern clusters disable auto-mount; verify `automountServiceAccountToken: false` in pods that do not need API access.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Namespaces are organizational, not security, boundaries** — require RBAC + NetworkPolicy + ResourceQuota to be real isolation; resources in `team-payments-dev` are invisible to `team-orders-prod` only if RBAC denies access.
- **Role is namespace-scoped, ClusterRole is cluster-wide** — start with Roles; create ClusterRoles only for platform admins managing nodes, namespaces, CRDs.
- **ServiceAccount RBAC controls what pods can do** — a pod's SA should have exactly the API permissions it needs; set `automountServiceAccountToken: false` on pods that do not call the K8s API.
- **ResourceQuota caps aggregate consumption per namespace** — prevents one team exhausting CPU, memory, or pod count; pair with LimitRange so pods without specs still get boundaries.
- **NetworkPolicy prevents pod-to-pod lateral movement** — default allows all traffic; a default-deny policy plus explicit allows is the safer posture in multi-tenant clusters.
- **`kubectl auth can-i` tests effective permissions** — verify before incidents, not after; `--as <user>` simulates another identity; `--as-group` simulates group membership.
- **Pod Security Standards in `restricted` mode** — per-namespace enforcement prevents privileged pods, root users, hostPath mounts for untrusted workloads.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
Namespaces and RBAC together enforce multi-team isolation in Kubernetes — namespaces provide the boundary, RBAC controls what each team can do within and across. The critical insight is that namespaces are not security boundaries; they are organizational boundaries reinforced by RBAC.

**Namespaces — organizational isolation**
- Every resource lives in a namespace; `kube-system` holds cluster components, `default` is where workloads land if you don't specify — always deploy to an explicitly created namespace, never `default`.
- Namespaces scope resource names — two teams can each have a Service named `payment-api` without conflict; DNS resolves them as `payment-api.team-a.svc.cluster.local` and `payment-api.team-b.svc.cluster.local`.
- `ResourceQuota` limits total CPU, memory, and object counts per namespace — the platform team controls how much each team can consume without per-deploy coordination.

**RBAC — who can do what**
- Four objects: `Role` (namespace-scoped), `ClusterRole` (cluster-wide), `RoleBinding` (assigns Role to subject in a namespace), `ClusterRoleBinding` (assigns ClusterRole cluster-wide).
- Least privilege: developers have `get/list/watch` on Pods and Deployments in their namespace, `create/delete` in non-prod only; prod is read-only and deploys happen via CI with a separate pipeline ServiceAccount.
- `kubectl auth can-i create deployments -n team-a --as developer@company.com` verifies effective permissions before incidents, not after.

**Production team separation**
- Separate namespaces per team and environment: `payments-prod`, `payments-staging`, `payments-dev`; RBAC for `payments-prod` is far stricter than dev.
- NetworkPolicy enforces communication boundaries — without them, any pod in any namespace can reach any Service cluster-wide; a policy allowing ingress only from expected namespaces prevents lateral movement after compromise.
- ServiceAccounts should be namespace-scoped with minimum permissions; pods that do not need API access set `automountServiceAccountToken: false` so the default token is not mounted inside the container.

**Quota and safety nets**
- `ResourceQuota` prevents one team from consuming the whole cluster; pair with `LimitRange` so pods without explicit requests/limits still get default boundaries and cannot bypass the quota system.
- Pod Security Standards at `restricted` enforcement prevents privileged pods, host-path mounts, and root users in untrusted namespaces — the replacement for deprecated PodSecurityPolicy.

speakable_v2.hook: Namespaces and RBAC together enforce multi-team isolation in Kubernetes — namespaces provide the boundary, RBAC controls what each team can do within and across.

beats.text: A developer runs kubectl delete deployment spring-app intending to clean up their dev environment. But their kubeconfig context was still pointed at the production namespace. The production deployment — with all its running pods — is gone. Every user gets connection errors. Recovery depends on how fast someone recreates the deployment. This disaster is entirely preventable with namespaces and RBAC. Namespaces create logical boundaries: team-payments-dev is completely separate from team-payments-prod. RBAC restricts what each user or ServiceAccount can do in.
Understanding of multi-tenancy patterns in enterprise Kubernetes

items: Namespaces are organizational, not security, boundaries — require RBAC + NetworkPolicy + ResourceQuota to be real isolation; resources in team-payments-dev are invisible to team-orders-prod only if RBAC denies access
Role is namespace-scoped, ClusterRole is cluster-wide — start with Roles; create ClusterRoles only for platform admins managing nodes, namespaces, CRDs
ServiceAccount RBAC controls what pods can do — a pod's SA should have exactly the API permissions it needs; set automountServiceAccountToken: false on pods that do not call the K8s API
ResourceQuota caps aggregate consumption per namespace — prevents one team exhausting CPU, memory, or pod count; pair with LimitRange so pods without specs still get boundaries
NetworkPolicy prevents pod-to-pod lateral movement — default allows all traffic; a default-deny policy plus explicit allows is the safer posture in multi-tenant clusters

beats.text: A developer runs kubectl delete deployment spring-app intending to clean up their dev environment. But their kubeconfig context was still pointed at the production namespace. The production deployment — with all its running pods — is gone. Every user gets connection errors. Recovery depends on how fast someone recreates the deployment. This disaster is entirely preventable with namespaces and RBAC. Namespaces create logical boundaries: team-payments-dev is completely separate from team-payments-prod. RBAC restricts what each user or ServiceAccount can do in each namespace: developers get read-write in dev, read-only in prod. The combination of namespaces + RBAC is what makes multi-tenant clusters viable. Without them, every team shares the same resource pool with unrestricted access — one team's misconfiguration takes down.

items: Giving developers cluster-admin, granting default ServiceAccount unrestricted access, or forgetting ResourceQuota so one team exhausts cluster
